projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Fred Osborne was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Melissa Parks
sp.p: Testing. Testing. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, and ten. Okay. If you would, say your name and what city and state you live.

sp.speaker: Fred Osborne
sp.p: Spell my name?

sp.speaker: Melissa Parks
sp.p: Just say it.

sp.speaker: Fred Osborne
sp.p: Fred Osborne.

sp.speaker: Melissa Parks
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: Fred Osborne
sp.p: Bessemer, Alabama.

sp.speaker: Melissa Parks
sp.p: Okay. What branch of military service were you in?

sp.speaker: Fred Osborne
sp.p: Navy.

sp.speaker: Melissa Parks
sp.p: What age were you when you entered it?

sp.speaker: Fred Osborne
sp.p: Eighteen.

sp.speaker: Melissa Parks
sp.p: And what age were you when you left the military?

sp.speaker: Fred Osborne
sp.p: Twenty-one.

sp.speaker: Melissa Parks
sp.p: And what was your rank?

sp.speaker: Fred Osborne
sp.p: I went in as a Apprentice Seaman, and I came out as a 1st Class Gunner's Mate.

sp.speaker: Melissa Parks
sp.p: What war were you in?

sp.speaker: Fred Osborne
sp.p: I was in World War II.

sp.speaker: Melissa Parks
sp.p: Did you receive any awards or medals while you were in?

sp.speaker: Fred Osborne
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Melissa Parks
sp.p: Tell any interesting stories that -- of your experiences that you had while you were in the military.

sp.speaker: Fred Osborne
sp.p: Well, interesting stories was -- that were interesting to me were -- was the -- when we was -- I was in the invasion of France at Normandy, and we were at Liverpool, England, and they converted the ship into a troop carrier. And we were not -- we were not told what we were going to do, but on the night before the invasion, they started -- all of a sudden there started to appear soldiers on the dock, and they marched right on up on our ship, plus all the other ships that was lined up along the docks, and everything was quarantined at that point. No one could enter onto the ship or no one could leave it for any reason whatsoever. And we pulled out during the night around o'clock in the morning, and we went out and hit the English Channel and went into Normandy. And that's where -- that was the most interesting. Well, that was the most -- that was the biggest story of any time that I was in the service. Needless to say, we were successful with the invasion, but there was an awful lot of people killed as they left the ship. As the soldiers left our ships, some of them were singing. Some were crying. Some were praying. Some were cursing, and because I guess they knew that possibly they never would return back again. And as they -- after they disembarked our ship, we had taken the position out some five miles from the coast. We backed off and pulled out about five miles, four to five miles from the coast, and we started in -- we started to bombard the beach, the beaches, and then on the 11 miles inland, and that was the limit of our guns, and then we stayed out with -- to take care of -- we switched our position from bombarding to working -- working and shooting at German planes that were coming over trying to bomb some of the ships that had men on them, still had men on them, so that was the -- that was the most interesting thing that I did, I guess, while I was in the service, other than I visited a lot of -- a lot of foreign ports and a lot of United States ports. The next -- the next the most exciting thing that I did while I was in the service, I made a round the world trip. I went through -- I went through the Suez Canal and through the Panama Canal. And we made a -- we made a round the world trip for some six months. It took us some six months to do it. The war ended. The war with Germany had ended, and the war with Japan ended, and we continued on our trip around the -- around the world. And we came back in to where I first caught the ship was in Norfolk, Virginia. That's where we came back to, and that was when I left the ship and was sent to Millington, Tennessee for discharge.

sp.speaker: Melissa Parks
sp.p: Okay. You mentioned you were a Gunner's Mate?

sp.speaker: Fred Osborne
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Melissa Parks
sp.p: Did that require any special training?

sp.speaker: Fred Osborne
sp.p: That required quite a bit of special training, which I had taken after I finished my boot camp in Great Lakes, Illinois, I was -- I was then put in OGU, outgoing unit, and was sent to Gulfport, Mississippi, where I taken my gunnery training and -- on how to fire the guns, and then how to do the mechanical works on the guns. And after we left -- after we left Gulfport, Mississippi, and I was put on a ship, why, then through -- through my knowledge of the guns that we -- that I was -- that I was on when we got on the ship, I was eventually promoted up at -- upward and to -- to a wartime temporary rating. I was not a permanent rating, but I was -- I had a temporary rating, which they gave to all people during the wartime that were not regular Navy people. I was -- I was a volunteer into the Navy. I volunteered into the Navy, and during the war and any ratings that you got after you finished your boot training and your gunnery training was temporary ratings that you were -- when you were discharged, you went back to your original rating, which mine was 1st Class Seaman. I had when I was -- I finished gunnery school, I was promoted to 1st Class Seaman and then worked my way up to 3rd and 2nd and 1st, to 1st Class Gunner's Mate, and then when I was discharged, I was discharged as my original rating.

sp.speaker: Melissa Parks
sp.p: What type of guns were you trained on or that you used?

sp.speaker: Fred Osborne
sp.p: Five inch 38-hydraulic guns and 20 millimeters. They were anti-aircraft guns and surface guns. They were surface guns and anti-aircraft guns.

sp.speaker: Melissa Parks
sp.p: Did you have to use guns?

sp.speaker: Fred Osborne
sp.p: Do what now?

sp.speaker: Melissa Parks
sp.p: Did you ever have to use them?

sp.speaker: Fred Osborne
sp.p: Did we have to use them? Yes. We did use them. We used them -- we used them several times while I was in the service. We had -- we had raids, air raids on us from time to time, and we had to use the guns for that, and then for -- to protect our ship, and I never fired up on another ship nor a submarine, but I did fire upon airplanes. And we also used them whenever -- during the invasion of Normandy.

sp.speaker: Melissa Parks
sp.p: Well, was there anything else that you wanted to say about anything in relation to World War II?

sp.speaker: Fred Osborne
sp.p: Well, relating to World War II, to a fella of my age which had never traveled anywhere in the United States or overseas, it was quite an education to go into the different ports overseas and, like, Liverpool, and ______ and Glasgow, Scotland, and into British Isles, and all of those type places. I saw an awful lot of the United States: Boston; New York; New Jersey; Baltimore; Norfolk, Virginia, and then went to the West Coast, and I went on the West Coast I was at San Francisco and San Diego, which I traveled, by traveling all those places, it was reliving my geography learning when I was in -- when I was in school. And it just brought it out to the front, brought everything out full circle as far as I was concerned. That's about all I can say other than I am proud that I was able to defend my country, and that I was able to come home alive.
